paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A considerable amount of research since the mid-1980s has examined what is known as children’s theory of mind. This is the ability to understand that people can hold different beliefs and representations of the world—a capacity normally evident by the age of four. This ability also appears to be absent in children with autism. Working out what another person is thinking is clearly important to both cognitive and social development. One influential explanation of autism is that affected children do not have a theory of mind (ToM). Consequently, the development of children’s ToM has attracted considerable attention.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Wimmer and Perner devised a ‘false-belief task’ to investigate this issue. They used toys to act out the following story. Maxi leaves some chocolate in a blue cupboard before going out. While he is away, his mother moves the chocolate to a green cupboard. Children are asked to predict where Maxi will look for the chocolate when he returns. Most children under four incorrectly answer that he will look in the green cupboard, whereas children over four tend to answer correctly that he will look in the blue cupboard. The incorrect answers suggest that younger children do not understand that Maxi’s belief no longer corresponds to the actual state of the world. They fail to appreciate that he will act on his belief rather than on how the world is actually organised.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Baron-Cohen devised a simpler version of the Maxi task in response to criticism that younger children might have been affected by the original story’s complexity and quantity of information. In the revised task, a child is shown two dolls, Sally and Anne, who have a basket and a box respectively. Sally places a marble in her basket and leaves for a walk. While she is out, Anne takes the marble from the basket and puts it in the box. Sally then returns, and the child is asked where she will look for the marble. The child passes by answering that Sally will look in the basket, where she left it, and fails by answering that Sally will look in the box, where the child knows it is hidden but Sally cannot. To pass, the child must understand that another person’s mental representation differs from their own and must predict behaviour from that understanding. Results from false-belief tasks have been fairly consistent: most normally developing children cannot pass them until around the age of four.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Leslie argues that, before 18 months, children interpret the world literally and rarely engage in pretence. He also argues that the cognitive system must distinguish pretence from reality; without this capacity, children could not separate imagination from the real world. Leslie suggests that pretend play becomes possible through a decoupler that copies primary representations into secondary ones. A child pretending that a banana is a telephone, for example, creates a secondary representation of the banana, manipulates that representation and uses stored knowledge about telephones to elaborate the pretence.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There is also evidence that social processes contribute to the development of ToM. Meins and her colleagues found that what they call mind-mindedness in mothers’ speech to six-month-old infants is related both to secure attachment and to later ToM ability. Mind-minded speech discusses an infant’s feelings and explains behaviour in terms of mental states, for example, ‘You’re feeling hungry.’

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Lewis investigated older children living in extended families in Crete and Cyprus. Lewis found that children who interacted socially with more adults, had more friends and had older siblings tended to pass ToM tasks at a slightly earlier age than other children. Young children are also more likely to discuss their thoughts and feelings with peers than with their mothers, so interaction with peers may provide a special impetus for ToM development. Dunn makes a similar point, arguing that peer interaction is more likely to include pretend play and to be more challenging because other children, unlike adults, do not make large adjustments for a child’s communicative needs.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: There is also concern that some aspects of the ToM approach underestimate children’s understanding of other people. Infants point to objects, apparently to redirect another person’s gaze and interest; they interact effectively with others, express ideas that oppose other people’s wishes and show empathy for others’ feelings. Schatz studied the spontaneous speech of three-year-olds and found that they used mental terms in situations involving a contrast—for example, between uncertainty about an object’s location and finding it, or between pretence and reality. Children’s social abilities therefore indicate that they distinguish mental states from external reality at ages younger than four.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Harris offers a different explanation: children use ‘simulation’. This involves putting oneself in another person’s position and predicting what that person would do. Success in false-belief tasks may therefore reflect children imagining what they themselves would do as a character in the story, rather than an ability to appreciate other people’s beliefs. Thinking about situations that do not exist is known as counterfactual reasoning.
